author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Identify anamorphic widescreen versus letterboxed PS2 output
summary: Use circles, character proportions, 2D overlays, and FMV boundaries to determine whether a title renders true anamorphic 16:9, embeds a letterbox inside 4:3, or needs separate aspect handling for gameplay and video.
heroAlt: PCSX2 automatic aspect-ratio switch example for widescreen gameplay and original 4:3 full-motion video

blocks.text: Measure geometry before choosing a viewport

A black bar does not by itself identify the intended format. A title can render anamorphic 16:9 into the same pixel raster as 4:3, draw a widescreen scene inside permanent top and bottom bars, or keep gameplay wide while prerendered FMV remains 4:3. Start with all emulator widescreen patches disabled and use an object whose shape is known, such as a circular gauge, moon, wheel, or symmetrical menu icon.
Do not crop bars until proportions are proven. Cropping a letterboxed 4:3 frame and then stretching it can remove subtitles, UI, or image content without producing true widescreen geometry.
Collect gameplay, menu, and FMV references

items: A gameplay frame containing a circle or clearly proportioned character.
A 2D menu or HUD with rectangular borders.
An FMV that begins soon after an in-game save.
Widescreen patches, zoom, overscan, and display stretch disabled.
The title serial, region, and its own aspect option recorded.
1. Cold-boot in 4:3 and capture the known circle, character, HUD, and visible bars.
2. Enable only the game's own widescreen option, if available, and repeat the same camera position.
3. Compare horizontal field of view: anamorphic gameplay should expand or preserve geometry rather than merely widen every object.
4. Play the FMV and note whether picture content, bars, and subtitles occupy a 4:3 or 16:9 region.
5. Return to the menu and confirm that 2D borders remain proportionate under the selected gameplay aspect.
6. When gameplay is wide but FMV is 4:3, use the emulator's documented automatic aspect behavior if available instead of one permanent stretch.
7. Test an official serial-matched widescreen patch separately from the game's own mode.
8. Record the accepted aspect for gameplay, FMV, and menus as three explicit results.

blocks.text: Anamorphic output stores a wide scene in a raster that must be displayed at a wider aspect. Letterboxed output stores the bars as part of a narrower presentation. PS2 games may mix those strategies by segment. Circles and field of view reveal geometry; FMV boundaries reveal whether video should switch back to 4:3.
The result must preserve proportions and content across every segment.

items: Known circles remain circular and character bodies are not widened.
Gameplay shows the intended horizontal field of view without cutting top and bottom content.
HUD and menus retain aligned borders and readable text.
FMV is neither stretched nor cropped and subtitles remain inside the visible frame.
Cold boot, FMV transition, and return to gameplay switch consistently.
Every object widens but field of view does not change: disable display stretch.
FMV fills 16:9 only after subtitles are cropped: restore its original aspect.
HUD moves while geometry improves: treat the patch as a separate validation task.
A patch targets another serial: remove it and verify the correct executable revision.

blocks.text: Disable the widescreen patch, select 4:3, remove zoom and overscan, and replay gameplay plus FMV. Restore the television input to pixel-accurate or no-overscan mode before creating a new aspect profile.
External displays may add their own stretch

A television can apply Wide, Zoom, Panorama, or overscan after Android outputs a correct frame. Validate a direct capture and the panel's input mode separately so display processing is not saved as an emulator workaround.
